body.text: One Nation recruit Barnaby Joyce says talks between his party and the Liberals have occurred but denies the two will consider a formal coalition.
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has dismissed Joyce's claim as a figment of his imagination.

Albanese and Trump pose for selfie
Anthony Albanese has also met with Donald Trump this evening at a welcome reception.
The prime minister took to social media to share a selfie of the pair, writing it was "always good to catch up to catch up with POTUS".
The pair caught up at the reception, hosted by the US president, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Albanese meets with Japanese counterpart for first time since melons gaffe
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has met with his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi for the first time since the furore over a gesture he made about two melons she gifted him.

The pair met on the sideline of the UN General Assembly in New York. The prime minister posted a picture of the pair on his Instagram, alongside other snaps from chats he had with other world leaders.
It's the first time the pair have met face to face since Albanese faced pressure to apologise for making light of two crown melons Takaichi gifted him when she visited Canberra in May.
He said the Japanese prime minister had brought a "couple of melons" as he made hand gestures in front of his chest. The Coalition called for the PM to apologise for the remarks.
At the time, Japan played down concerns over the controversy.
No word on if it was raised during their chat!
Call to slash new political donation caps
New political donation caps will leave too much money in Australian politics and disadvantage emerging political candidates.
The Grattan Institute policy brief released today says a $90 million political party spending cap, due to take effect in 2027, is “too high”.
It proposes slashing the total cap to $40 million, a limit that would still exceed the $30 million cost of previous national campaigns.
“Capping electoral expenditure puts a ceiling on money in politics – and, if well-designed, can reduce its influence,” says Grattan Institute democracy expert Kate Griffiths.
It also recommends new independents and new parties should be allowed to spend up to $1.2 million on their campaigns, while keeping an $800,000 electorate limit for established candidates.
Joyce 'clutching at straws': Hume
Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume has rubbished claims that there have been talks between the Coalition and One Nation about a potential confidence and supply deal to form government.
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce said discussions were underway but denied the two would consider a formal coalition.
Speaking to News24, Senator Hume denied knowledge of the talks and said that Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Nationals leader Matt Canavan were also unaware of the discussions.
"I have absolutely no idea exactly what it is that he is discussing or who he is discussing it with. Perhaps he could be a little more explicit about that," she said.

"I am pretty sure that this is Barnaby clutching at straws. "I don't know what Barnaby's motives are. Perhaps he's got some sort of post-purchase dissonance moving to One Nation. I can understand that."
"I am pretty sure that this is Barnaby clutching at straws.
"I don't know what Barnaby's motives are. Perhaps he's got some sort of post-purchase dissonance moving to One Nation. I can understand that."
Bowen jets off to India and Saudi Arabia
Amid a global oil crisis and with the world climate conference looming, Energy and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen has headed overseas to talk energy security.

Bowen will stop in India to meet with his counterparts and visit the Jamnagar oil refinery in Gujarat — which is the world's largest refinery — and convene a roundtable with clean energy industry representatives.

In Saudi Arabia, he will hold meetings with Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud about the evolving situation overseas, including the closure of the East-West pipeline, and its implications for global energy security.

The pipeline had become a critical alternate route for oil since Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, carrying about 4 per cent of the world's supply prior to the recent attacks that forced its closure.
Australia is exposed because many of the Asian refineries it relies on for imported fuel use Saudi crude.
Bowen is also planning to visit the world's largest solar farm while in Saudi as he seeks to highlight the importance of electrification in future energy security, which is a key priority for COP31.
Libs dismiss One Nation deal as 'figment' of Joyce's imagination
So how have Liberal MPs responded to Barnaby Joyce's claim the party is in talks with One Nation for a confidence and supply deal?
Well, Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson dismissed it as a figment of Joyce's imagination.
"I know that Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan have confirmed that that's not the case. So, I think it's a figment of his imagination," he told News24.
"I get that he's got regrets about joining One Nation. I do understand that. After betraying his community, his party, and his leader, I understand that."
Liberal backbencher Simon Kennedy said he was willing to work with anyone to get rid of Labor but he did not think the opposition would formalise a coalition with One Nation.
"I don't think we're seeking to have any formal alliances with anyone else," he told ABC's Radio National Breakfast.

Joyce says One Nation, Libs discussing confidence and supply pact

"Of course we are having conversations and everybody knows quite obviously that there's no prospect in current polling that the Coalition can form government, nor can One Nation," he told News24 this morning.
"And obviously, it's not about becoming a coalition. "We don't want to be in a coalition … to be quite frank. But there will be a discussion."
"And obviously, it's not about becoming a coalition.
"We don't want to be in a coalition … to be quite frank. But there will be a discussion."
So what does that mean? It would mean that One Nation would agree to offer confidence and supply to the Coalition should they get close enough at the next election to form a minority government.
Joyce wouldn't confirm who he'd spoken to within the Coalition.

Earlier, Shadow Tim Wilson shrugged the whole thing off as a "figment of his [Joyce's] imagination". Joyce responded with a barb of his own, calling Wilson a "clown" and questioning whether he could count.
Bragg defends decision to go it alone on call for super rethink
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Bragg has defended his call for a superannuation rethink after suggesting retirement savings should be able to used as collateral for a mortgage.
The shadow housing minister pushed the idea, among others, in a speech yesterday where he called for a debate about super being used for home ownership.
Such a proposal has not been adopted by the shadow cabinet. Bragg says the debate is occurring internally within the Coalition but that shouldn't stop him.

"It's important in public life not to waste the time you've been given by the people. And I think it's critical that we gets the facts out there because, as I say, the Labor Party is desperate to run a scare campaign."
'We live in a free society': Bragg fine with US intervention in algorithm reforms
Coalition frontbencher Andrew Bragg has echoed the Trump administration’s "censorship" concerns, after the US embassy’s rare submission to the government’s draft duty of care laws.
"I think there is a risk of censorship. There is a risk of bestowing too much power onto unelected bureaucrats," Bragg told ABC Radio National Breakfast.

"There is a risk of too much regulation, which may not actually have any great impact on our economy or our society. So I have to say I share some of the concerns, but obviously Australia will make its own judgments on these things."

The Coalition has previously aired concerns about the proposed changes, saying they give a "blank cheque for political censorship" to the minister in charge, and warning they pose a threat to free speech.
When asked if it was appropriate for the US to be weighing in on our domestic laws, Bragg said it wasn’t unusual for Australia to hear from other countries in relation to legislative reform.
“I think it's fine. I mean, we live in a free society, or at least we used to, and people are allowed to express a view. Maybe they'll be censored by the new laws," he said.
Was the government's migration policy modelled?
Daniel Mulino was unable to say whether the government modelled the impact of the government's migration re-think on wages and employment.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke last week released the long-awaited plan to tighten visa rules for international students and backpackers while cracking down on efforts to remove overstayers.
The assistant treasurer told ABC's Radio National Breakfast there was "rigorous" consideration to the impact of the policy as he sidestepped repeated questions on if the policy had been modelled.
"What I would say is that this is a policy that balances the need to bring migration down to sustainable levels with the broader economic impacts," he says.
"And that's the appropriate frame in which this should be considered."
Housing needs own policy not just a super re-think: Mulino
Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino has taken a whack at the opposition's "strange" policy process after the shadow housing minister floated using super as collateral for a mortgage.
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Bragg set the cat among the pigeons yesterday with the idea, something both he and leader Angus Taylor clarified was not opposition policy.
Speaking with ABC's Radio National Breakfast this morning, Mulino said he was "not impressed" with Bragg's latest thought bubble.

"But interestingly with all of these ideas, Angus Taylor is sitting on the sidelines, saying he's got an open mind. So none of these ideas seem to come forward with any official support or sanction from shadow cabinet or leadership," he says.

"It's a very strange process. There's very little modelling, there's very little process, there's very little genuine policy rigour, but there's also — it doesn't seem to be any kind of authorisation from the top. "I'm not impressed at all with the latest round of ideas."

"It's a very strange process. There's very little modelling, there's very little process, there's very little genuine policy rigour, but there's also — it doesn't seem to be any kind of authorisation from the top.
"I'm not impressed at all with the latest round of ideas."
Mulino says the issue of housing and homeownership needs to be dealt with through dedicated policy, not through a rethink of retirement savings.
Mulino doesn't see problem with US intervention in digital duty of care
Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino has been asked about the United States's rare intervention over draft digital duty of care legislation.

Late yesterday the Trump administration warned the legislation would be an "extraterritorial censorship of protected speech" and called on Australia to exclude US social media companies from plans to give users more choice about their algorithms.
"I would expect … that we would apply this to digital platforms no matter where their origin is," Mulino told ABC Radio National Breakfast.
"I certainly don't see a problem with the US or other governments expressing views around novel policy developments."
He said some of the criticism about the proposed reforms didn't acknowledge that social media users would be given a choice to opt in or out of the algorithm.
"We have highlighted the need for protections in relation to what can at times be addictive algorithms, algorithms that can create harm," he said.
Albanese declines to directly respond to Trump's speech
US President Donald Trump rejected a push from a coalition of middle powers, including Australia, for tougher AI controls.
In a speech to the UN General Assembly, Trump declared the US would not stifle the development of the technology.
Asked what he made of the address, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese didn't want to directly respond to the speech.

"We have put forward a strong position ... I'm proud of what we have done on social media and the fact that the European Union have now announced major reform as well, joining the more than 20 countries who've taken action," he says.
Pressed if he was disappointed by Trump's rejection for internationally coordinated safeguards, Albanese took a wait and see approach.
"We'll wait and see what comes out of the meeting between President Trump and President Xi [Jinping]. It's good that they're meeting and it's good that this is on the agenda."
Albanese will attend a welcome reception hosted by Trump shortly. The PM says he looks forward to engaging with the president there.

PM doubles down on digital duty of care after Trump administration criticism
It's been a busy afternoon (morning for us) for Anthony Albanese in New York, who has just held a press conference on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
The prime minister was asked about the Trump administration's criticism of the government's digital duty of care legislation.
"I will always stand up for Australia's national interests and the digital duty of care is something we've foreshadowed for some period of time," he says.
"It's not about giving government control; it's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices, which is why it's framed in that way."
Another reporter later asks if Trump administration had undermined Albanese tech push on the world stage.
"Not at all," he said.

"The fact is that we have released an exposure draft of legislation. We haven't even introduced the legislation before the parliament. We'll engage constructively," he said. "I hope the whole of parliament supports it. This should not be a partisan issue."

PM responds to criticism of algorithm legislation
Just circling back to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's speech to an event on the sidelines of UN General Assembly.

The prime minister was a co-host for the Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI event in New York. He used a speech at the event to discuss his government's plan for people to be able to opt out of social media algorithms.
The move is part of the government's digital duty of care bill, which would force platforms to take actions to mitigate and respond to harms caused by digital platforms.
The move has been criticised by the opposition and social media companies. Late yesterday, the Trump administration warned the policy would be "extraterritorial censorship of protected speech".
Albanese responded to the criticisms more broadly in his address this morning.
"The criticism of this legislation is not surprising, that [it] is about government control," he says.
"It is the opposite of that. It's about giving everyone control over their own lives.

"And it's an inevitable next stage because whilst today we are concentrating on the impact on children, the truth is this is having an impact on our entire society and how it functions with misinformation, disinformation.

"With the increased polarisation that we're seeing as well in the political system, where people are moving away from the centre and more and more to the extremes, be they of the left or the right. And that is why we think that this is a very positive move that we are being put forward."
Albanese meets with UK PM Andy Burnham
By pool reporter Andrew Brown in New York
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has held his first face-to-face meeting with British counterpart Andy Burnham, who took the top job in July.
Meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Albanese joked that he was pleased Burnham had made good on his agreement to become a South Sydney NRL supporter.
Onto more serious matters, he also noted AUKUS was central to ties between the two countries.
Burnham complimented Albanese for the work he'd done on the teen social media ban, noting the UK would take its own approach to getting teens off the platforms.
Albanese developed a close relationship with Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, during his time in office.

PM warns leaders not to repeat mistakes of social media with AI
No country can manage the risks of artificial intelligence "alone", Anthony Albanese has told world leaders in a call for international cooperation to regulate the technology.
The prime minister has used a speech on the sidelines of the United Nations to warn tackling risks like child exploitation, biological weapons or rogue AI incidents requires global coordination.

As a co-host of the Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI event in New York, Albanese argued artificial intelligence can "bring great good" but only if "humans are in control of it".
He has promoted Australia's social media age ban as a way of giving children breathing space online, noting more than 20 countries are considering similar laws.
The PM has argued a coordinated approach on AI is also required.
"The idea, as some have argued, that AI will create perfection is something that I think is very misdirected," he says.
"We do have the power, we have the agency but, importantly as well, we have the choice.

"But the choices that we have as leaders will determine what happens for the next year and the next decade. "Because if we leave it like I think we did on social media … we should have moved earlier. Let's not make the same mistake. Let's learn form it and make sure that we shape AI in the interests of humanity".

Trump weighs 'big decision' on Iran, rejects AI push in major UN speech on 'American power'

US President Donald Trump has used a speech at the UN to portray "American power" as the solution to the world's problems, defending his ongoing war with Iran and declaring he now must decide whether to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic.
Trump also said the US would reject any international scheme to put controls on artificial intelligence.
The comment came just a day after 22 world leaders, including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, signed a statement calling for global guardrails.

Opening of UNGA is people watching on steroids as world leaders roll in

On the floor of the iconic United Nations General Assembly hall, the world's most powerful people and their aides are brought to attention by a man carving his way through the crowd enthusiastically, waving a brass handbell above his head.

The opening session of the 81st General Assembly has begun. It is the largest gathering of leaders in one place and was set up to maintain and enforce international rules in the aftermath of World War II. In 2026, it's under serious strain from superpowers rewriting the rules in their favour.
From the gallery overlooking the circular hall — for the journalists (including this correspondent) lucky enough to have secured a ticket — it’s people watching on steroids.

Anthony Albanese shakes hands with Canada’s Mark Carney before Julie Bishop — former foreign minister and now special envoy on Myanmar — makes a surprise appearance and sidles up beside him for a chat.

Once seated (on the same table as Austria and two rows behind Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine), Albanese and Penny Wong are joined by Australia’s ambassador to the UN, James Larsson, ambassador to the US Greg Moriarty, the PM’s international adviser Rod Hilton and DFAT boss Jan Adams.

Everyone patiently listens to UN secretary-general António Guterres’s defiant final address (for which he was given a standing ovation), and then Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, (who gets top billing due to longstanding tradition) before the man everyone is here for, Donald Trump, enters the room.
Ninety minutes late, he walks straight up to the rostrum. And now, the show begins.
Albanese meets with Korean counterpart
Reporting by pool reporter Katina Curtis in New York.
The meeting was preceded by an extended negotiation between officials over whether the leaders would shake hands twice or once for media and protocol purposes.
Lee greeted Albanese by asking when he had arrived in New York.
Speaking via a translator, Lee then noted that due to the ongoing conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, Korea had faced "various challenges" with energy supply chain disruptions.
"But thanks to the help and cooperation of Australia, our energy market has been stabilised," he said.
Albanese thanked him for the warm welcome and said Australia and Korea were "great friends" who shared a similar world view of support for multilateral institutions, security and stability.
"We rely upon each other as well for economic security. Particularly, we regard the role that we play in supplying secure energy to Korea as being very important," he said.
Albanese ended his remarks by saying he looked forward to welcoming Lee to Australia early next year.
They shook hands twice.
